item.title: Entrepreneurial Ecosystems in Emerging Economies
item.content:encoded:
Ioana Stefan, Mälardalen University

Ikenna Uzuegbunam, Howard University

Brett Anitra Gilbert, American University

Wim Vanhaverbeke, Antwerp University

Kadigia Faccin, Fundação Dom Cabral

Yanbo Wang, University of Hong Kong

This special issue addresses entrepreneurial ecosystems in emerging economies, where new ventures face distinctive obstacles including institutional weakness, high uncertainty, and limited market access. While research on entrepreneurial ecosystems has expanded significantly, most studies focus on developed nations, leaving a knowledge gap about how these ecosystems function in the Global South and other emerging regions.

The call welcomes research that balances Global North and Global South perspectives, examines ecosystem emergence and development over time, applies systems thinking, and investigates how digitalization shapes entrepreneurial activity in resource-constrained contexts. Contributors are encouraged to explore how entrepreneurial ecosystems address institutional voids, support different types of entrepreneurs, and contribute to sustainable development goals.

item.title: International Entrepreneurship In An Age Of Persistent Disruption
item.content:encoded:
Olga Petričević, University of Calgary

Christos N. Pitelis, National and Kapodistrian University of Athens

Stratos Ramoglou, University of Bristol

Catherine L. Wang, Brunel University of London

Shaker A. Zahra, University of Minnesota

This special issue examines how entrepreneurial firms internationalize amid systemic disruptions from geopolitical, technological, and institutional shocks. Rather than treating disruption as occasional crisis, it positions persistent turbulence as the default operating condition reshaping how ventures compete globally. The focus shifts from traditional questions about early entry timing to how firms adapt, survive, and reconfigure while designing new competitive advantages.

The call seeks research integrating strategy, international business, entrepreneurship, and innovation to understand how entrepreneurial agency interacts with systemic shocks. It invites theoretical and empirical work examining strategic reconfiguration, dynamic capabilities, and knowledge mobility in fragmented global contexts, investigating how ventures develop dexterity, orchestrate cross-border relationships and digital infrastructures, navigate regulatory complexity, and build resilience amid technological volatility and geopolitical realignment.

  • Strategic dexterity and resource orchestration

  • Digital infrastructures and interorganizational alliances
  • Non-market and political capabilities
  • Cross-border knowledge creation and protection

item.title: Mobilizing, Organizing, and Exploiting Entrepreneurial Judgment Within Ecosystems
item.content:encoded:
David B. Audretsch, Indiana University Bloomington

Maksim Belitski, University of Reading

Rosa Caiazza, Parthenope University of Naples

Nicolai J. Foss, Copenhagen Business School

Donald Siegel, Arizona State University

This special issue examines how entrepreneurial judgment operates within modern business ecosystems rather than in isolation. While prior research has focused on individual decision-making and single firms, contemporary entrepreneurship involves complex collaborations, alliances, and digital platforms where multiple stakeholders must coordinate their judgments under uncertainty. The issue seeks to understand how entrepreneurs communicate their private and tacit knowledge to ecosystem participants, and how various governance arrangements facilitate or hinder this coordination.

The guest editors invite submissions that bridge entrepreneurship, strategy, and organizational research to explore the mechanisms through which judgment is mobilized, organized, and exploited across ecosystem actors. Key questions include how entrepreneurs convey tacit judgment while managing risks of knowledge leakage, how ecosystem governance structures affect stakeholder coordination, and whether heterogeneous judgments can outperform consensus-based decision-making. The issue aims to consolidate fragmented literature across disciplines into a cohesive multilevel research agenda.

Potential topics
